title: Freyja: Desire, Magic, and Power
subtitle: A goddess whose roles resist one label

learningObjectives.text: Explain what Snorri and Grímnismál say about Freyja and the slain.
Compare the prose account with its cited poetic passage.

prose.author: Snorri Sturluson
prose.locator: Freyja and Folkvang in Gylfaginning; local text normalized characters 86916-87244
prose.excerpt: Freyja is the most famous of the goddesses. She has in heaven a dwelling which is called Folkvang, and when she rides to the battle, one half of the slain belong to her, and the other half to Odin. As is here said: Folkvang it is called, And there rules Freyja. For the seats in the hall Half of the slain She chooses each day;
prose.note: Verbatim Rasmus B. Anderson translation excerpt; whitespace normalized.

poem.author: Anonymous Old Norse poets
poem.locator: Grímnismál, stanza 14; local text normalized characters 149488-149647
poem.excerpt: 14. The ninth is Folkvang, | where Freyja decrees Who shall have seats in the hall; The half of the dead | each day does she choose, And half does Othin have.
poem.note: Verbatim Henry Adams Bellows translation excerpt; whitespace normalized.

narrativeBlocks.title: A share of the slain
narrativeBlocks.body: Snorri's Gylfaginning says Freyja chooses half of those slain in battle for seats in Folkvang; Odin receives the other half.

narrativeBlocks.title: Snorri's prose account
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (translated; whitespace normalized): “Freyja is the most famous of the goddesses. She has in heaven a dwelling which is called Folkvang, and when she rides to the battle, one half of the slain belong to her, and the other half to Odin. As is here said: Folkvang it is called, And there rules Freyja. For the seats in the hall Half of the slain She chooses each day;”

narrativeBlocks.title: The poetic stanza
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (translated; whitespace normalized): “14. The ninth is Folkvang, | where Freyja decrees Who shall have seats in the hall; The half of the dead | each day does she choose, And half does Othin have.”

narrativeBlocks.title: Compare the witnesses carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: Anderson's edition identifies the verse as Grímnismál 14. Treat the prose and poem as related source testimony, not as two unrelated confirmations of a historical afterlife system.

narrativeBlocks.title: Do not flatten the claim
narrativeBlocks.body: These passages describe a literary division of the battle-dead. They do not establish that every Norse community held one uniform belief about the afterlife.

quiz.prompt: In Gylfaginning, who chooses half of those slain in battle?
quiz.explanation: Snorri assigns half to Freyja and half to Odin.
